method: Full original article text read in author-uploaded ResearchGate web presentation and compared with publisher/NIH abstract. Primary Aquinas and RAINN texts also checked. This is targeted claim-by-claim appraisal, not blanket signoff of every sentence in these three dossiers. PDF page image verification was unavailable; original text was inspected as HTML.

claims: Genital responses are reported in some nonconsensual sexual experiences
Occurrence is supported for included cases; universal response or rate is NOT supported.
24,501 initial database hits, 10,684 deduplicated, 13,817 screened plus 77 additional; counts refer to records not 13,894 people.
Eight articles and one book contributed relevant data
Papers published 1977–2019; sparse and heterogeneous underlying observations.
The pooled study figures do not estimate population prevalence
Authors explicitly prohibit prevalence inference from percentages due to incomparable study designs and sampled populations.
Published abstract lists 136 male survivors while results section uses denominator 135
Abstract p.2305 vs Reported Frequencies p.2309
No justified resolution for one-person discrepancy; user-facing question deliberately avoids counts.
The reviewed data do not establish circumstances or mechanisms of arousal in a particular survivor
Suggested explanatory theories remain hypotheses; do not claim universal reflex, inevitable pleasure, or cause.
Involuntary arousal, lubrication or orgasm does not equal consent
What Is Enthusiastic Consent?, following positive yes examples
RAINN is a specialist support source, not a population-prevalence study or an opposing moral author.
Voluntary human acts differ from external bodily events against the will
Does not prove physiological frequency and is not a source for precise legal sexual consent rules.
A response does not render the person responsible for an assault
I-II q.6 aa.4–5 read alongside RAINN consent statement
Responsibility for a coercive act cannot be inferred from an involuntary bodily reaction.
Informed meaningful consent requires capacity and voluntariness
Article lists sober/alert and freely communicating; avoid claiming a legal BAC threshold.
Severe impairment and unconsciousness can prevent meaningful sexual consent
No global alcohol-dose or intoxication threshold was supplied.
Not every circumstance involving alcohol establishes the same mental capacity
Capacity varies; neither Aquinas nor RAINN establishes specific local legal thresholds.
Forcible conduct against the will is involuntary
Do not equate mere absence of struggle with a positive act of will.
Two equally intoxicated persons need not have equal subjective culpability
I-II q.6 aa.4–8 and individual-intention assessment
Particular culpability and legal liability depend on facts; rule is not a blanket excuse.
Avoid sexual activity where consent capacity is doubtful
Safety guidance, not clinical statistical conclusion nor a ruling in a concrete legal dispute.
Passion can diminish free deliberation without invariably removing grave personal responsibility
The Aquinas source does not evaluate a specific individual's degree of freedom.
Prior voluntary causes of later passion remain relevant
Avoid formulae that blame victims for bodily reactions beyond the will.
Knowingly chosen vice must be distinguished from involuntary passion
I-II q.77 a.8; compare I-II q.78
The adjacent q.78 requires separate original-source citation, not a direct quote from q.77 alone.
Repetition cannot prove the subjective mortal guilt of a particular person
Spiritual and clinical assessments of a person require individual context and specialist care where appropriate.
Empirical claims about compulsive sexual behaviour require clinical research, not addiction-by-analogy
Aquinas does not independently certify current clinical diagnoses, prevalence or treatment outcomes.
